promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

learningObjectives.title: Change of state and specific heat capacity
Ideal gas molecules and the gas laws

questions.q: Which equation correctly defines the density of a substance?
questions.explain: Density (ρ) is defined as mass per unit volume, ρ = m/V.

questions.q: What is the SI unit of density?
questions.explain: In SI units mass is in kilograms and volume in cubic metres, giving density in kg/m³.

questions.q: A metal block has a mass of 240 g and a volume of 30 cm³. What is its density?
questions.explain: Density = mass ÷ volume = 240 ÷ 30 = 8 g/cm³.

questions.q: Which equation relates pressure to force and area?
questions.explain: Pressure is the force acting normally per unit area, p = F/A.

questions.q: What is the SI unit of pressure?
questions.explain: One pascal equals one newton per square metre (1 Pa = 1 N/m²).

questions.q: Which equation gives the pressure difference at a depth h in a liquid of density ρ?
questions.explain: The pressure due to a column of liquid is p = hρg, where g is the gravitational field strength.

questions.q: Water has a density of 1000 kg/m³. Taking g = 10 N/kg, what is the pressure due to the water at a depth of 2 m?
Why does the pressure in a liquid increase with depth?
options: There is a greater weight of liquid above pressing down
The liquid becomes denser lower down
Gravity is stronger at greater depths
The liquid moves faster lower down
questions.explain: The deeper you go, the greater the weight of the liquid column above, so the pressure is higher.

questions.q: What is the specific heat capacity of a substance?
options: The energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg by 1°C
The energy needed to melt 1 kg of the substance
The temperature at which a substance boils
The energy stored in 1 kg of the substance
questions.explain: Specific heat capacity is the energy required to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a material by 1°C.

questions.q: Which equation gives the change in thermal (internal) energy when a substance is heated?
questions.explain: Change in thermal energy = mass × specific heat capacity × change in temperature.

questions.q: How much energy is needed to raise the temperature of 2 kg of water (specific heat capacity 4200 J/(kg°C)) by 10°C?
Why does the temperature stay constant while a pure substance is melting or boiling?
options: The energy supplied is used to break bonds between particles rather than raise temperature
No energy is being supplied during the change of state
The substance stops absorbing energy once it starts to melt
The thermometer cannot detect the temperature change
questions.explain: During a change of state the energy goes into separating particles, so the temperature does not rise until the change is complete.

questions.q: What is the unit of specific heat capacity?
questions.explain: Specific heat capacity is measured in joules per kilogram per degree Celsius, J/(kg°C).

questions.q: Which statement best describes the arrangement of particles in a solid compared with a gas?
options: Solid particles are close together in a fixed regular arrangement, while gas particles are far apart and move randomly
Solid particles are far apart and move freely, while gas particles are closely packed
Both solids and gases have particles in fixed positions
Gas particles are held in a regular lattice while solid particles move randomly
questions.explain: In a solid the particles vibrate in fixed positions, whereas in a gas they are widely spaced and move quickly in random directions.

questions.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes evaporation from boiling?
options: Evaporation happens only at the surface and at any temperature, while boiling happens throughout the liquid at a fixed temperature
Evaporation happens throughout the liquid, while boiling happens only at the surface
Both occur only at the boiling point of the liquid
Evaporation requires more energy than boiling for the same liquid
questions.explain: Evaporation is a surface process that occurs at any temperature, whereas boiling occurs throughout the liquid at its boiling point.

questions.q: What is the value of absolute zero on the Celsius scale?
questions.explain: Absolute zero, the lowest possible temperature, is approximately -273°C, equal to 0 K.

questions.q: A gas is at a temperature of 27°C. What is this temperature on the Kelvin scale?
questions.explain: T(K) = temperature in °C + 273 = 27 + 273 = 300 K.

questions.q: What causes the pressure exerted by a gas on the walls of its container?
options: Gas molecules colliding with the container walls
Gas molecules sticking to the container walls
The weight of the gas molecules resting on the walls
Attractive forces between the molecules and the walls
questions.explain: Gas pressure results from the many collisions of fast-moving molecules with the container walls.

questions.q: For a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature, how are pressure and volume related?
options: Pressure is inversely proportional to volume, so p₁V₁ = p₂V₂
Pressure is directly proportional to volume
Pressure is proportional to the square of the volume
questions.explain: At constant temperature, halving the volume doubles the pressure, so p₁V₁ = p₂V₂ (Boyle's law).

questions.q: A fixed mass of gas has a volume of 200 cm³ at a pressure of 100 kPa. At constant temperature it is compressed to 50 cm³. What is the new pressure?
questions.explain: Using p₁V₁ = p₂V₂: p₂ = (100 × 200) ÷ 50 = 400 kPa.
